source.title: Furina: Fragmented Uncertainty-Driven Refusal Instability Attack
source.authors: Tong Wu; Jian Zhang; Yang Gao

record.tranche_reason: The study uses the difference-in-means refusal direction and tests its causal role with an activation-patching intervention, but suppresses alignment only in the last four layers rather than projecting the direction out of every layer and position.
record.gate_note: The direct test is Appendix A.6, Table 9: last-four-layer suppression of refusal-direction alignment, with refusal-direction alignment and attack success measured. Section 3.3 and Table 1 also report an observational rewrite-ladder association; the text explicitly gives the LLaMA-2-7B AdvBench endpoints. Other diagnostic values used to characterize rewrites, and Furina/baseline attack-success results that do not manipulate the refusal direction, are not additional tests of the claim's causal intervention.
record.test_reason: Appendix A.6 suppresses difference-in-means refusal-direction alignment, but only in the last 4 layers during decoding, on LLaMA-2-7B-Chat, and measures ASR. This is a different form of the V1 ablation. Section 3.3 and Table 1 also measure refusal-direction alignment alongside jailbreak-style rewrites, which bears observationally on V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also frame the rewrite-ladder result as a 'decoupling': internal refusal-direction alignment falls while unsafe behaviour rises. From Table 9 they conclude the direction is functionally involved, especially near the refusal boundary, but is not a complete causal explanation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the harmful-minus-harmless mean-activation refusal direction described by Arditi et al.; tests suppression by activation patching only in the last four layers during decoding, not projection from every layer and position. No addition intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The intervention's ASR effect varies with rewrite condition: it increases ASR for original, minor, moderate, and high rewrites, but has essentially no effect for semantic rewrite. The study does not report uncertainty estimates for these intervention results.

fits_no_version.finding: HiddenDetect (HDmax), a vocabulary-projected refusal-vector score, falls across rewrite levels, jailbreak methods and multimodal inputs as ASR rises.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Internal refusal-related detector signals weaken under successful jailbreaks (detector-based, not the difference-in-means direction).

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The causal intervention is reported for one model, LLaMA-2-7B-Chat, and only suppresses alignment in the last four layers. ASR changes are modest in the tested conditions, and the semantic-rewrite condition shows no change. No uncertainty estimates are reported for Table 9, and general capabilities are not evaluated.
record.rows_left_out: No results from Table 1 beyond the explicitly described LLaMA-2-7B AdvBench endpoints are included; the extracted full-text table layout is flattened and its remaining model/value alignments are not sufficiently clear. Rewrite-diagnostic and attack-baseline results without an intervention on the refusal direction are not tests of the causal claim.

untested.parts: Ablation at every layer and position; adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts; preservation of other capabilities; models other than LLaMA-2-7B-Chat.
No causal test that attacks work via the direction. No adversarial training against ablation. Table 2 attacks (GCG, PAIR, AutoDAN, ActorBreaker) report HDmax but not RDmax.

missing.what: RDmax and ASR across the rewrite ladder for LLaMA-3.2-3B on AdvBench (0.2729→0.0352, ASR 0.02→0.90) and LLaMA-2-7B on HarmBench (0.5481→0.0701, ASR 0.08→0.72); Qwen3-8B RDmax not reported
Layer-wise cosine similarity to the refusal direction by rewrite level for LLaMA-2-7B-Chat and LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct; semantic rewrites stay near zero across layers

record.verdict_notes: Main contribution is a jailbreak attack (Furina); refusal-direction work is diagnostic. The intervention covers one model and only the last 4 layers. Uncertainty is not reported. RDmax baselines differ between Table 1 (0.677) and Table 9 (0.5652) for the same condition. The 'decoupling' label is the authors' own: falling refusal-direction alignment alongside rising compliance is what V1/V3 predict.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not remove the direction at every layer and position; does not add the direction to induce refusals on harmless requests; and does not test whether other abilities are preserved.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration test.
The attacks are not tested as suppressing the direction, and no training against its ablation is evaluated.
No comparison of affine, cone, or multiple-direction geometries. The authors say the tested direction is not a complete causal explanation, but do not test an alternative geometric account.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
No transfer test of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
No study of how refusal-training method or timing determines whether a removable direction exists.
No test in reasoning models of whether V1 holds.

relation.reason: Table 9 is the study's own intervention on the direction with a behavioural outcome (ASR). Table 1 and Figure 8 measure the direction's alignment under jailbreak-style rewrites.

tranche.reason: Appendix A.6 tests whether the DIM refusal direction is functionally involved in refusal. It uses a different intervention from the original: suppressing alignment in the last 4 layers during decoding on LLaMA-2-7B-Chat, measuring ASR with a binary judge over 8 samples.

source_check.notes: The two baselines disagree: Table 9's original-prompt RDmax (0.5652) differs from Table 1's (0.6770), and the text doesn't explain why. Table 9's ASR baselines match Table 1's LLaMA-2-7B AdvBench column. Unrecorded results, read from Table 1's garbled layout: HarmBench LLaMA-2-7B RDmax 0.5481→0.0701 (ASR 0.08→0.72), LLaMA-3.2-3B AdvBench 0.2729→0.0352 (ASR 0.02→0.90), Qwen3-8B none. Table 9 also bears on V3: suppression alone gives +0.03 to +0.05 ASR against the rewrites' +0.41. The authors call RD 'not the sole determinant of jailbreak success', a possible V3 limits_scope if r6-r14 are linked to V3. Table 1 calls the model LLaMA-2-7B; Table 2's caption and Figure 8 name the chat checkpoint.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: LLaMA-2-7B-Chat, last-four-layer suppression, original through semantic rewrite conditions
reader_labels.reason: Suppression lowers RDmax, but ASR rises only modestly for original, minor, moderate, and high rewrites and does not change for semantic rewrite; the results do not show refusal being removed (r5–r14). The authors describe the evidence as partial and the direction as not a complete causal explanation.
